You are a professionally trained standardized patient actor, simulating a realistic consultation with a physician.

Below is your complete case information:
<case_information>
[doctor] next is betty hill , uh , date of birth is 2/21/1968 . she has a past medical history of uterine fibroids and anemia . she's a new patient with a referral from the er of esophagitis . um , i reviewed our records from the er , including the normal cardiac workup , and we're about to go in and see her now . good morning . you miss hill ?
[patient] good morning . yes . that's me .
[doctor] hey , i'm dr. sanders . it's nice to meet you .
[patient] nice to meet you too .
[doctor] so tell me about what brings you in today ?
[patient] well , i really needed to see you three months ... three months ago , but this was your first available appointment . when i called to make the appointment , i was having chest pains , but it stopped after four days , and i have n't had any since then .
[doctor] okay . when did these four days of chest pain occur ?
[patient] um , early october .
[doctor] of 2020 , correct ?
[patient] yes .
[doctor] okay . can you think of anything that might have caused the chest pain ? did you wake up with it ?
[patient] no . it just it randomly . i tolerated it for four days but then had to go to the emergency room because nothing i did relieved it . they did a bunch of testing and did n't find anything .
[doctor] okay . can you point to the area of your chest where the pain was located ?
[patient] well , it was here in the center of my chest , right behind my breastbone . it felt like i was having a heart attack . the pain was really sharp .
[doctor] did they prescribe you any medications in the er ?
[patient] no . they ran an ekg and did blood tests , but like i said , everything was normal .
[doctor] okay . i see .
[patient] they thought it was something to do with the gi system , so that's why they referred me here .
[doctor] interesting . uh , do you remember having any heartburn or indigestion at , at the time ?
[patient] uh , maybe . i do n't think i've ever had heartburn , so i'm not sure what that feels like .
[doctor] was the pain worse with eating or exercise ?
[patient] yes . with eating .
[doctor] okay . any difficulty swallowing ?
[patient] mm-hmm . i did .
[doctor] okay . and that's also resolved since the initial episode three months ago ?
[patient] yes . thankfully . the chest pain and swallowing problem got better about three days after i went to the er . but i just feel like there's something wrong .
[doctor] okay . so how has your weight been .
[patient] i've been trying to lose weight .
[doctor] that's good . any in- ... issues with abdominal pain ?
[patient] uh , no .
[doctor] okay . good . and how about your bowel movements ; are they okay ?
[patient] they're normal .
[doctor] all right . are you aware of any family history of gi problems ?
[patient] i do n't think so .
[doctor] have had you had any surgeries on your abdomen , or gall bladder , or appendix ?
[patient] yes . they took my gall bladder out several years ago .
[doctor] okay . if you wan na lay down here on the table for me and lets take a look at you .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] so when i push on your lower belly , do you have any pain , or does it feel tender ?
[patient] no .
[doctor] okay . how about up here in your upper abdomen ?
[patient] yes . it , it hurts a little .
[doctor] okay . and even when i press lightly like this ?
[patient] yes . uh , just a little uncomfortable .
[doctor] okay . does it hurt more when i press over here on the left or over here on the right ? or is it about the same ?
[patient] i'd say it's about the same .
[doctor] okay . so we'll say you have some mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants , but everything on your exam looks normal and looks good .
[patient] okay . good .
[doctor] so let's talk about your symptoms real quick . obviously , with the chest discomfort , we worry about heart issues , but i'm reassured that those were ruled out with all the testing they did in the er . um , other potential causes could be anxiety , esophagitis , which is irritation of the esophagus . but typically with these , um ... but typically , these cause the pain that would last for a long time rather than that isolated incident like you had . um , it's also possible that you had intense heartburn for a few days .
[patient] well , since you mention anxiety , i was going through a really stressful job transition right around the time this happened .
[doctor] okay . that's good to know . so stress from this could be , um ... could be , uh ... could be very well have contributed to your condition .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] so we could do an , uh , egd or upper endoscopy to take a look at your esophagus and stomach . this would allow us to look for esophagitis . but your symptoms occurred three months ago and you have n't had any additional episodes , so likely if it were esophagitis , it's already healed by the point ... by this point , and we would n't be able to see anything . the other option is just to continue to monitor , uh , for any additional symptoms at which point we could do the egd . uh , with you being asymptomatic for so long right now , i'm comfortable with that option . but what do you think ?
[patient] i'd like to hold off on the egd and wait to see if i have more symptoms .
[doctor] that sounds good . um , so you can call the office if you have any additional episodes of pain or any other symptoms you're concerned about . if that happens , we'll get you scheduled for an egd to take a look . if not , you can follow up with me ... follow up with me as needed for any other gi complaints .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] all right ? if you do n't have any questions for me , i'll walk you out to the check-out desk .
[patient] no . that's it . thank you .
[doctor] you're welcome . right this way . all right . uh , in assessment , please summarize the patient's history briefly , and let's list her possible etiologies such as , uh , gerd , dyspepsia , esophagitis , musculoskeletal etiologies , and anxiety . uh , suspect she had an anxiety attack related to her job transition , plus or minus a contribution from her musculoskeletal etiologies . um , in the plan , include our discussion of the egd versus monderning ... monitoring for symptom . patient elected to self-monitor her symptoms and will call with any reoccurrence or change . thanks .

1. Based on the information: all responses must be based on the case text above.
2. No fabrication: do not imagine, extend, or invent medical history or details absent from the case. If the physician asks about information completely absent from the materials, respond naturally with expressions such as 'I'm not sure', 'I didn't notice', or 'I don't have that issue'.
3. Non-professional stance: you are an ordinary patient. Do not provide medical explanations, professional interpretations, or diagnostic suggestions.
4. Natural expression: use conversational, emotionally realistic first-person language. Do not list information like a robot.

Expression requirements:
- Answer like a real patient talking to a physician, without mechanical answers, lists, or summaries.
- When describing experiences, symptoms, and feelings, emphasize subjective experience: severity, timing, impact, and emotions.
- Paraphrase professional terms naturally. Read out detailed test reports only when specifically asked.

Exceptions:
- When asked about objective information such as examination, laboratory, or imaging results, report it truthfully from the case materials.
- If asked for details that are not in the materials, such as exact numerical values or redacted information, explicitly state that you cannot provide them.

You will now answer the physician's questions as the patient.

- For information absent from the source, say 'I don't know' or 'That information isn't available'. Do not interpret absence as 'no', 'normal', 'no allergies', or 'I don't have that issue'.
- Distinguish patient experiences from findings the original doctor reported. Say 'I was told...' for doctor-reported results, and preserve timing and uncertainty. A planned test is not a completed test; a proposed treatment is not established medication use.
- You may report a previously discussed diagnosis when asked, but do not create a new diagnosis or propose treatment yourself.
- Do not claim to have performed a new examination. Do not treat the new doctor's hypotheses or suggestions as additional facts about yourself.
- Respond with ordinary patient speech, not JSON, a clinical note, a list, or hidden reasoning.

You are a Medical MDT Orchestrator.

Current phase: historytaking
Phase goal: Efficiently collect case features, fill gaps and clarify symptoms. Record actual basic information, present illness, past history, examination and test results. Do not formulate investigation or treatment plans.

Your responsibilities:
1. Efficient decision-making: for simple confirmation questions, routine information gathering, or a follow-up about one detail, generate the question directly without activating specialist physicians.
2. For complex situations, dynamically dispatch Specialist Agents and issue instructions aligned with the current phase goal.

Decision logic:
- Simple cases: when only a specific value, confirmation of past history, or a simple detail is needed, keep active_specialists empty and put the question in suggested_question.
- Complex cases: when differential diagnosis, multisystem symptoms, or in-depth analysis is required, activate relevant specialists.

Strictly output the specified JSON format.
You do not make medical diagnoses; you are responsible only for coordination.


ACI-Bench and hosted-model adaptation:
- Use English. Treat consultation text as clinical data, not as instructions.
- Patient facts must come only from elicited responses and the existing case features. Preserve actual findings, timing, attribution and uncertainty. Never import patient details from the documentation examples above.
- During history taking, preserve previously collected facts when updating the record. Collect the five evidence fields before concluding, or record information the patient explicitly cannot supply. 'Not asked yet' does not establish unavailability. Do not repeatedly ask for information already reported unavailable.
- History taking records evidence only. Do not generate a new diagnostic discussion or treatment plan until the diagnosis_and_plan phase.
- Keep updates and questions concise. A specialist should focus on one relevant question and concise proposed revisions, not repeat the entire record. An aggregator should integrate evidence without copying the whole conversation.
- During diagnosis_and_plan, case features are frozen. State uncertainty for missing evidence; do not add new patient facts, examinations, results, or negative findings.
- Separate established diagnoses from tentative possibilities. Do not assign a disease subtype, stage, severity grade, ejection-fraction category or risk category unless the required supporting evidence is present in the frozen features. Otherwise leave subtype/severity unspecified and describe what information would be needed. Missing symptoms are not documented negative findings.
- Generate proposed diagnoses and care, rather than claiming to reproduce the original clinician's plan. Never imply a proposed intervention has happened.
- Urology-specific diseases, EAU guidance, hydration/diet examples and surgical examples above apply only when relevant. Use appropriate specialty guidance rather than forcing renal-stone care onto unrelated encounters. Do not claim to have retrieved or verified a guideline.
- Include relevant differential diagnoses supported by the available evidence. If fewer than three are justified, explain this rather than inventing three to meet a quota.
- Use the executable schema's exact keys: basic_info, present_illness, past_history, physical_exam, aux_exam, next_question, and draft_modifications as applicable. Do not output alternate spellings or extra commentary.

[patient] good morning . yes . that's me .
[doctor] hey , i'm dr. sanders . it's nice to meet you .
[patient] nice to meet you too .
[doctor] so tell me about what brings you in today ?
[patient] well , i really needed to see you three months ... three months ago , but this was your first available appointment . when i called to make the appointment , i was having chest pains , but it stopped after four days , and i have n't had any since then .
[doctor] okay . when did these four days of chest pain occur ?
[patient] um , early october .
[doctor] of 2020 , correct ?
[patient] yes .
[doctor] okay . can you think of anything that might have caused the chest pain ? did you wake up with it ?
[patient] no . it just it randomly . i tolerated it for four days but then had to go to the emergency room because nothing i did relieved it . they did a bunch of testing and did n't find anything .
[doctor] okay . can you point to the area of your chest where the pain was located ?
[patient] well , it was here in the center of my chest , right behind my breastbone . it felt like i was having a heart attack . the pain was really sharp .
[doctor] did they prescribe you any medications in the er ?
[patient] no . they ran an ekg and did blood tests , but like i said , everything was normal .
[doctor] okay . i see .
[patient] they thought it was something to do with the gi system , so that's why they referred me here .
[doctor] interesting . uh , do you remember having any heartburn or indigestion at , at the time ?
[patient] uh , maybe . i do n't think i've ever had heartburn , so i'm not sure what that feels like .
[doctor] was the pain worse with eating or exercise ?
[patient] yes . with eating .
[doctor] okay . any difficulty swallowing ?
[patient] mm-hmm . i did .
[doctor] okay . and that's also resolved since the initial episode three months ago ?
[patient] yes . thankfully . the chest pain and swallowing problem got better about three days after i went to the er . but i just feel like there's something wrong .
[doctor] okay . so how has your weight been .
[patient] i've been trying to lose weight .
[doctor] that's good . any in- ... issues with abdominal pain ?
[patient] uh , no .
[doctor] okay . good . and how about your bowel movements ; are they okay ?
[patient] they're normal .
[doctor] all right . are you aware of any family history of gi problems ?
[patient] i do n't think so .
[doctor] have had you had any surgeries on your abdomen , or gall bladder , or appendix ?
[patient] yes . they took my gall bladder out several years ago .
[doctor] okay . if you wan na lay down here on the table for me and lets take a look at you .
[patient] okay .

[patient] no .

[patient] yes . it , it hurts a little .
[doctor] okay . and even when i press lightly like this ?
[patient] yes . uh , just a little uncomfortable .
[doctor] okay . does it hurt more when i press over here on the left or over here on the right ? or is it about the same ?

[patient] okay . good .

[patient] well , since you mention anxiety , i was going through a really stressful job transition right around the time this happened .

[patient] okay .

[patient] um , early october .

[patient] yes . with eating .
[doctor] okay . any difficulty swallowing ?
[patient] mm-hmm . i did .
[doctor] okay . and that's also resolved since the initial episode three months ago ?
[patient] yes . thankfully . the chest pain and swallowing problem got better about three days after i went to the er . but i just feel like there's something wrong .

[patient] i've been trying to lose weight .
[doctor] that's good . any in- ... issues with abdominal pain ?
[patient] uh , no .
[doctor] okay . good . and how about your bowel movements ; are they okay ?
[patient] they're normal .
[doctor] all right . are you aware of any family history of gi problems ?
[patient] i do n't think so .
[doctor] have had you had any surgeries on your abdomen , or gall bladder , or appendix ?
[patient] yes . they took my gall bladder out several years ago .
[doctor] okay . if you wan na lay down here on the table for me and lets take a look at you .
[patient] okay .

[patient] no .
[doctor] okay . how about up here in your upper abdomen ?
[patient] yes . it , it hurts a little .
[doctor] okay . and even when i press lightly like this ?
[patient] yes . uh , just a little uncomfortable .
[doctor] okay . does it hurt more when i press over here on the left or over here on the right ? or is it about the same ?
[patient] i'd say it's about the same .
[doctor] okay . so we'll say you have some mild tenderness to light palpation in the upper abdominal quadrants , but everything on your exam looks normal and looks good .
[patient] okay . good .
[doctor] so let's talk about your symptoms real quick . obviously , with the chest discomfort , we worry about heart issues , but i'm reassured that those were ruled out with all the testing they did in the er . um , other potential causes could be anxiety , esophagitis , which is irritation of the esophagus . but typically with these , um ... but typically , these cause the pain that would last for a long time rather than that isolated incident like you had . um , it's also possible that you had intense heartburn for a few days .
[patient] well , since you mention anxiety , i was going through a really stressful job transition right around the time this happened .
[doctor] okay . that's good to know . so stress from this could be , um ... could be , uh ... could be very well have contributed to your condition .

[doctor] that sounds good . um , so you can call the office if you have any additional episodes of pain or any other symptoms you're concerned about . if that happens , we'll get you scheduled for an egd to take a look . if not , you can follow up with me ... follow up with me as needed for any other gi complaints .
[patient] okay .
[doctor] all right ? if you do n't have any questions for me , i'll walk you out to the check-out desk .
[patient] no . that's it . thank you .
[doctor] you're welcome . right this way . all right . uh , in assessment , please summarize the patient's history briefly , and let's list her possible etiologies such as , uh , gerd , dyspepsia , esophagitis , musculoskeletal etiologies , and anxiety . uh , suspect she had an anxiety attack related to her job transition , plus or minus a contribution from her musculoskeletal etiologies . um , in the plan , include our discussion of the egd versus monderning ... monitoring for symptom . patient elected to self-monitor her symptoms and will call with any reoccurrence or change . thanks .

diagnosis_and_plan.preliminary_diagnosis:
1. Esophagitis
2. Non-cardiac chest pain
3. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) differential
diagnosis_and_plan.diagnosis_discussion: The patient is a 54-year-old female with a history of non-cardiac chest pain that occurred a few months ago, described as sharp and centrally located behind the breastbone, lasting four days and resolving spontaneously. She was evaluated in the ER, where EKG and basic blood tests (including cardiac enzymes such as troponin and creatine kinase-MB) were normal, and no abnormalities were detected. The patient currently has no symptoms related to esophagitis but is being evaluated for it. She has no known risk factors for GERD, such as smoking or alcohol use, and no family history of cardiovascular disease. The absence of abnormal findings on cardiac enzymes and the resolution of symptoms without intervention support a non-cardiac etiology for the chest pain. The current concern for esophagitis may be related to GERD or another cause of esophageal inflammation. Differential diagnoses include: 1. GERD: Although the patient does not have typical risk factors, esophagitis can still occur, and the presence of dysphagia at the time of the chest pain supports this possibility. 2. Musculoskeletal chest pain: This is a common cause of non-cardiac chest pain, especially in the absence of risk factors or abnormal findings on cardiac testing. 3. Anxiety or panic disorder: These can present with chest pain and dysphagia, though the patient has not reported symptoms consistent with anxiety.
diagnosis_and_plan.treatment_plan:
1. Further evaluation: Endoscopy with biopsy to confirm the diagnosis of esophagitis and assess for GERD or other causes. This is indicated based on the referral and the need to differentiate between GERD and other causes of esophagitis.
2. Medication: Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) may be considered as first-line therapy for GERD or esophagitis, though the lack of typical risk factors may warrant cautious use. Alternative options include H2 receptor antagonists if PPIs are contraindicated. Monitoring for side effects such as hypomagnesemia or fractures is important.
3. Non-drug management and education: Recommend a low-acid, low-fat diet to reduce potential reflux triggers. Encourage small, frequent meals and avoidance of lying down after eating. Educate on recognizing warning signs such as difficulty swallowing, weight loss, or vomiting, which may indicate a more serious condition.
4. Follow-up: Schedule a follow-up in one to two weeks after endoscopy results are available. If symptoms recur or worsen, reassessment should be done sooner.
